en: Explanatory Preface to the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* (The Treatise on Entering Right Reasoning).

The fundamental cause of all phenomena (*dharma*) is called "right reasoning" (*nyāya*). That which penetrates the fundamental cause of all phenomena is called "right knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*). Reasoning is manifested through knowledge;

the thesis (*pakṣa*) relies upon the elucidation of reasoning. With knowledge as the means of entry and right reasoning as the object of entry, the Bodhisattva realizes true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Through inference (*anumāna*), there exist true means of establishment (*sādhana*) and true means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). By means of wisdom one illuminates the principles, and thereby awakens oneself and others;

thus it is called "The Entrance into Correct Principles through the Science of Reasoning" (*Hetuvidyā-praveśa-tattvārtha*). For instance, by establishing *tathatā*, one enters the correct principle of *tathatā*;

by establishing *vijñaptimātra*, one enters the correct principle of *vijñaptimātra*; and by establishing impermanence, one enters the correct principle of impermanence. If one is not a person who has realized the truth, then...
To open one’s mouth and have thirty-three [objections] follow in succession, establishing formal syllogisms (pramāṇa)—is this not difficult?

It is like the principle that when rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments issue from the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords fold their hands and await his commands, and the world is well-governed.

But when these issues issue from the feudal lords or high ministers, the four barbarian tribes invade one after another, and the people have no place to set their hands or feet. Therefore, having examined this treatise:
It is like a commoner perusing the genealogical records of emperors; though he may know the order of the ancestral ranks, he cannot claim descent from the divine lineage.
Or again, it is like one who thoroughly knows every article of the Three Thousand Laws, yet, being no judicial officer, seeks to impose punishment upon the guilty—who would submit to such a verdict?
Thus, what the student must urgently pursue is the realization of the Truth; indeed, the pursuit must lie in the realization of the Truth.

How true! This commentary on the *Dharmadhātustava* was compiled by drawing upon the teachings of various masters. Reading it to survey the extensive texts is like holding up a mirror to reflect one’s own face.
Therefore, I did not dare to keep it secret, but have carved it into woodblocks to publish for the benefit of all who are determined to realize the truth.

Outline of the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* Exegesis of the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhijie of Zhuili.
The outline is divided into four parts. △ First, the explanation of the title.
Regarding the *Nyāyapraveśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering Right Reasoning): these six characters constitute the title of this treatise. As for "treatise" (*śāstra*), one—

The "words" (*akṣara*) are the expressive texts; the aforementioned five characters are the expressed meanings. That is to say, the correct principles of *hetuvidyā* (logic) are manifested through treatises (*śāstra*).
Thus, the meaning is revealed by the treatise, and the treatise is named after its meaning. When both text and meaning are manifested together, the subject and object are designated as a unity;

hence it is called the *Nyāyamukha-prakaraṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering the Correct Principles through Logic). Within these aforementioned five characters, the first two characters are the [subject].
"Entering the knowledge of causes. The latter two characters refer to the correct principle (*samyaktva-yukti*) into which one enters. "Entering" encompasses both the subject and the object;
this is because, through the truth of the knowledge of causes, one attains entry into the correct principle. Thus, Qingliang said: "Causes" refers to the causes for the arising of the myriad dharmas;
"knowledge" refers to the wisdom that contemplates the fundamental causes of phenomena. This refers to the various worldly discourses and diagrams...
He clearly understood and attained unimpeded mastery over the seals and insignia of writing, as well as earth, water, fire, and wind—the causes of all phenomena.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata elucidates both mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their conditions;
even the various things before his eyes—such as pines being straight and thorns being crooked, cranes being white and crows being black—he fully understands their underlying origins."
All of these use wisdom to illuminate the fundamental cause of all phenomena; therefore, it is called "Prakāśya" (Illumination through Causality). Yongming said:

"The 'True Principle' refers to the essential substance and meaning of the original reality of all phenomena. This means that if one is deluded regarding the nature of awakening, the spiritual luminosity will be obscured, and one will fail to realize the true cause of all phenomena.
Consequently, emotional attachments lead to entangled errors. Now, we must sever the false doctrines of the wild and ignorant, and block the path of heterodoxy."
When the inverted mind is overturned, one enters into the fundamental reality of all phenomena; this is precisely self-awakening and entry into the correct principle (*nyāya*).

Furthermore, regarding "entering the correct principle by means of the logical reason" (*hetu*): the "reason" refers to the middle member among the three members of a syllogism, for the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason, and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are inseparable.
"Clarification" (*prakāśana*) refers to the wisdom produced in the opponent, which is induced by hearing the logic established by the proponent.

Therefore, the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "The one true nature of suchness (tathatā) is the subject (dharmin). It is established as the thesis (pakṣa) that it necessarily conforms to conditions.

The reason (hetu) is: because it is the equal basis of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma). The concordant example (sapakṣadṛṣṭānta) is like space. Furthermore, the lower section of the treatise states: "Sound is the subject.
It is established as the thesis that it is necessarily impermanent. The reason is: because it is produced (kṛtaka). The concordant...
It is like the example of a jar. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* asks: "What is called the field of logic (*hetuvidyā*)? It refers to all matters involved in the investigation of meanings.
The commentary explains: "The established phenomena are called 'investigated meanings,' while the phenomena that accord with them are the means of investigation."
"Names" refers to all things that exist. All things that exist are precisely *hetuvidyā* (the science of logic).

These are all dharmas established through illumination by means of causes, which cause those who hear them to give rise to correct knowledge regarding the inferred meaning, thereby realizing impermanence and so forth.

This is precisely what leads others to awakening and entry into the correct principle. Therefore, it is said: "By means of many statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), [one] reveals..."
Because those who ask have not yet understood the meaning, they inquire: "When establishing a formal argument (*vāda-pramāṇa*), the three members are complete;

since the result (*phala*) is clear and not explicitly raised, why do you speak only of the means of cognition based on reason (*hetu-pramāṇa*)? The answer is: Because the reason (*hetu*) is the primary factor among the means of cognition. Thus, the *Daichao* states:

"Within inference (*anumāna*), there is that which is accepted and that which is not accepted. To establish what is not yet accepted, there must necessarily be a means of establishment; this means of establishment is the reason (*hetu*). As for the object of establishment (*sādhya*):

This constitutes the fruit. Since the thesis (*pakṣa*) is manifested through the reason (*hetu*), its meaning becomes clear; thus, it is called *Hetuvidyā* (Logic). There is no contradiction or obstacle in this principle.

Furthermore, this treatise refers to the investigation and analysis of false theses and the thorough clarification of correct principles; hence it is titled the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering Correct Reasoning).
Now, a treatise consists of both the thesis and the commentary; this is a thesis-treatise. Moreover, there are two types of theses: first, the thesis itself.
The various schools establish and refute meanings based on the propositions (*pakṣa*) and their constituent elements; it is through these that this treatise is established. Thus, Cien (Ci'en) said:

"Originally, these were only the Buddha’s teachings, scattered throughout the various sūtras; they have been gathered together here to form [this work]. Second, regarding the proponents of the system (*siddhāntin*):

this refers to Kaśyapa Mātanga and Vasubandhu, who definitively established the three members [of the syllogism]. Thus, Yongming said: "At the beginning of the kalpa, Kaśyapa and Mātanga first distinguished between the true and the fallacious; and furthermore..."
Vasubandhu restated the formal rules; yet, although the governing framework was established, the subtle nuances remained undifferentiated.

Then Dignāga, having been exhorted by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, composed the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* (Compendium on Valid Cognition). Although this work is based on [Vasubandhu’s] school, its meaning is nonetheless complete.
Question: Since the principles of proof, refutation, and so forth are already fully prepared in the various sūtras, let alone in the numerous śāstras, for what reason [was this treatise composed]?
Why was this treatise composed? The answer is: it is for the purpose of skillfully adapting to the needs of the times and providing those who prefer concise texts with an easy means of entry.
Thus, Nāgārjuna’s *Upāyahṛdaya* (Treatise on the Heart of Skillful Means) states: "In order to discern and uphold the reality within the meanings of proof and refutation."
Therefore, this treatise was composed. △ Next, the author is identified.
It was composed by the Bodhisattva Śaṅkarasvāmin.
Śaṅkarasvāmin is translated here as "Lord of Heaven" (Tiānzhǔ), because the postscript refers to him as the Lord of Heaven. Alternatively, he is called [Kārttikeya].

"Luó" (羅) is merely a difference in the dialects of the Sanskrit sound. As for the meaning of "Bodhisattva," since it has already been explained extensively in various commentaries, I shall not elaborate further here.
It means "to create" or "to construct. △ Third, the explanation of the translators.

The circumstances of the translation by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Xuanzang, are fully detailed in the postscript. △ Fourth, the explanation of the main text is divided into three parts. First, establishing the gates to provide a general synthesis.
The proof, the refutation, and their fallacies serve only to enlighten others; direct perception, inference, and their fallacies serve only to enlighten oneself.
Thus, the essential points of all treatises are subsumed herein.
This establishes eight gates to comprehensively encompass the essential meanings of all treatises. As for the eight gates: the "real" comprises four gates, and the "semblance" contains four gates.
First, the real means of establishment (*sādhana*) refers to presenting valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to an opponent, wherein the three members [of the syllogism] are complete and clear.

1. A genuine *dūṣaṇa* (refutation) is that which brings about understanding in the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), namely by rejecting an incomplete *pramāṇa* and pointing out errors in the members [of the syllogism]. 2.

A genuine *sādhanābhāsa* (fallacious proof) is that which, when presenting a *pramāṇa* against an adversary, lacks one of the three members or contains errors, and thus does not bring about understanding in the opponent. 3.
A fallacious *dūṣaṇābhāsa* (pseudo-refutation) is that which falsely rejects [the proof] as incomplete and points out errors in the members, yet fails to bring about understanding in [the opponent].

5. True direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is so called because it is the arising of correct cognition regarding objects such as form, which operates within its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
6. True inference (*anumāna*) is so called because it is the arising of corresponding cognition that observes an object by means of various signs (*liṅga*). 7.

Fallacious direct perception is so called because it is a conceptualizing cognition that operates erroneously with respect to an object, such as when one perceives a jar, a garment, or the like. 8. Fallacious [inference]... [text truncated]
Inference (*anumāna*) refers to the arising of a contrary understanding regarding the object to be inferred through the cognition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Regarding "awakening others":
this is because, through proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), one is able to initiate in others meanings that they have not yet understood. Regarding "awakening oneself":

this is because, through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference, one is able to induce the two types of wisdom—those involving true and fallacious existence and non-existence. All of the above is cited from the *Qīngliáng Shù* (Commentary by Qingliang).

The *Chao-yi-shi* (Exegesis on the Meaning of the Commentary) states: "Thus, below" refers to the two benefits of the eight sections, which can comprehensively encompass the meanings of establishment, refutation, and so forth found in various treatises.
Next, there are eight parts for the detailed explanation according to the sections. First, the section on the true means of proof (*sādhana*) is divided into two.
First, the general heading of the means of proof is divided into two. First, a brief explanation of the means of proof.

In this context, the multiple statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth are called the "proof" (*sādhana*). This is because, by means of these multiple statements—the thesis, the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—the meaning that remains uncomprehended by those who inquire is revealed.

"Among these" refers specifically to the *Vādavidhi* (Treatise on Debate). "And so forth" includes other reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, the collection of multiple statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason, and example is called the "prover" (*sādhana*).

This is briefly explained below under the section on the thesis: it is called the prover because, by means of the multiple statements of thesis, reason, and example, it reveals a meaning not yet understood by another.
Furthermore, there are two types of provers: first, the three members (*trirūpa*) as the prover; [the second being the five-membered syllogism].

It is established that the collection of multiple statements consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*udāharaṇa*) is called the "means of proof" (*sādhana*). Alternatively, the reason and the example alone constitute the means of proof;

for the reason is the very reason belonging to the thesis, and the example is subsumed within the reason. It is through the reason and the example that the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) is established.

Therefore, this constitutes the "proof" (*sādhana*). Here, the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) itself is taken as that which is to be established. Now, examining the treatise, the proof encompasses all three [members].
II. A detailed explanation of the proof, divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the thesis.

In this context, the thesis (*pakṣa*) refers to a subject that is commonly recognized and a qualifier that is commonly recognized, which, by virtue of their distinct nature, are intended by the proponent to be established as the property to be proven.
This is called the thesis. For example: "Sound is impermanent."
"Among these" refers to the true establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Thesis" means that which is revered and that which is primary;

it refers to taking the meaning one reveres as one's primary principle and expressing it through words so as to awaken others—this is called a thesis. Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"It is the proclamation to others of the meaning accepted by oneself as that which is to be established, causing them to understand it."

Because they are understood, they are termed the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) and so forth. Regarding "the subject (*dharmin*) that is universally established and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) that is universally established":

the subject is that which is presented first, namely dharmas such as form (*rūpa*). Since dharmas such as form serve as the basis for the thesis, they are also called the "basis of the thesis" (*pakṣāśraya*).
Regarding the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), this is precisely the qualified (*viśeṣya*). The qualifier is the latter member (*uttara-pada*), meaning the essence of the thesis (*sādhya*) itself.

Because one relies upon this essence and is entirely free from all faults, it is called "the well-established subject" (*prasiddha-dharmin*) and "the well-established qualifier" (*prasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*).
As for the phrase "because of its distinct nature," this explains the aforementioned point: that while the thesis is strictly a single entity, it is nevertheless said to possess [these two aspects].

"Regarding the term 'the dharma that can distinguish': it is because it relies on the distinction of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, it is explained as establishing the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

That is to say, this true *sādhana* (proof) is called a true *sādhana-pakṣa* because both the subject (*dharmin*) and the distinguishing attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) are fully established, owing to their distinction from the nature of a pseudo-proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
The phrase 'according to one's own [view]' and so forth concludes the meaning of the thesis. That is to say, when..."

When the preceding [elements] and the succeeding [elements] are unified into one place, and according to the proponent’s own intention and acceptance regarding the nature of that which is to be established, it is called a "thesis" (*pakṣa*).
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "In this context, that which is intended by one's own mind as the object to be established is designated as the thesis.
Question: What is the difference between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the essence of the thesis? Answer: Master Xuanzang says: Although it is the qualifier...

This constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). When it is established and the proponent accepts it, yet the opponent has not yet disputed it, it is still merely the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*) and is not yet called the essence of the thesis (*pakṣasvabhāva*).

If the combination of the prior term and the subsequent term is accepted as the thesis by the proponent, but is not accepted by the opponent, such that the proponent and opponent dispute it together, this is named the essence of the thesis.
If the proponent and opponent have not yet disputed it, it remains the basis of the thesis. Thus, the *Qixin ji* (Record of the Awakening of Faith) states: [text follows].

It is said: "Based on the existence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*," which is precisely this meaning. For example, as in the formulation of a thesis (*pakṣa*), one says: "Sound is the *dharmin* (the subject;

this is the universally accepted *dharmin*)," and "it is definitely impermanent" is the thesis (*sādhya*; this is the universally accepted qualifier). If the three members [of the syllogism] are complete, it should be stated:
"Because it is a product (*kṛtakatvāt*); the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is like a jar; the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is like space. This, then, is...
The proponent definitively accepts impermanence as the subject (*pakṣa*) of the thesis.

If one follows the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the refutation of an opponent's position, this thesis specifically refutes the opponent’s argument that "sound is eternal. The opponent’s formal inference (*pramāṇa*) states: "Sound is a functional entity (*dharmin*);

it is established as eternal" (this commits the fallacy of the non-establishment of the specific qualifier). The reason (*hetu*) is "because it is produced" (this commits the fallacy of contradicting the specific nature of the property). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*)...
"Like space" (this constitutes the fault of the establishing property not being established). This opponent intends for "eternal" to be the body of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Since the proponent's argument is that [space] is impermanent, if the opponent does not recognize that space is non-produced (*akṛtaka*), then [the reason] will not apply to the subject, and the example will be dissimilar;
thus, the argument that sound is eternal cannot be established. Part Two: Explaining the Reason (*hetu*). This is divided into two sections.
First, the number is indicated and the characteristics are enumerated.

There are three characteristics of the reason (*hetu*). What are these three? They are: (1) being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), (2) being necessarily present in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and (3) being entirely absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*).
The "reason" (*hetu*) refers to that by which something is derived; it is the characteristic of being conducive, beneficial, and dependent.
That is to say, regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) established, to state its essential nature and its attributes is called the reason. Therefore, the *Daichao* states:

"Because there exists this basis from which [the thesis] is derived, the nature of the dharma of the thesis is revealed, and only then does the result of the thesis become clear. By this, it is shown that...
The thesis (*pakṣa*) that is established is of a single, uniform flavor. That which is able to establish the thesis is called the reason (*hetu*).

As for the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), they refer to the similar (*sapakṣa*), the dissimilar (*vipakṣa*), and pervasion (*vyāpti*). Pervasion is the general characteristic, while the similar and dissimilar are the particular characteristics. The phrase "What are these? below interrogates and enumerates the three characteristics.
"Pervasive nature of the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) means that the probans (*hetu*) is entirely a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*).

For example, the "produced" reason (*kṛtakahetu*) is entirely impermanent. Because it is a property of the subject, the reason pervades the properties of the subject; this is called a "decisive reason" (*niścitahetu*).

If there were even the slightest degree of non-pervasion, it would be a "doubtful reason" (*saṃdigdhahetu*). "Certainty of existence in similar instances" (*sapakṣe sattvam*) means that the reason is coextensive with the thesis.

Thus, the thesis exists by virtue of its reason. Therefore, Nāgārjuna’s treatise states: "The thesis does not exist without a reason. Even if there is a slight lack of uniformity, it is not definitively existent.

For example, impermanence is only definitively established when "being produced" serves as its reason. Regarding the phrase "the heterogeneous instance (*vipakṣa*) is entirely devoid of the nature [of the probandum]":

this means that at the locus where the thesis is established, the property to be proven is completely absent from the homogeneous instances (*sapakṣa*). If there were even the slightest trace of it, then—
It is not universally absent. Only when one establishes "permanence" by taking "not being produced" as the reason does one obtain universal absence.

Thus Nāgārjuna said: "In this context, there are only two kinds of reasons: namely, being present in all similar instances (sapakṣa) and being universally absent in all dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
Alas! The discourse on similarity and dissimilarity has been muddled for a long time, yet those who are deluded have ultimately...
To exclude the same by means of a different property is truly due to not understanding the intent behind establishing "sameness" (*sādharmya*) and "difference" (*vaidharmya*).

In establishing a property based on the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the necessity of both sameness and difference arises for three reasons. First, it is because one fears that the property to be established might become confused or conflated.

One employs sameness so as not to rely on difference, fearing that if one relies on difference, one cannot definitively establish existence. One employs difference so as not to rely on sameness, fearing... [that if one relies on sameness, one cannot definitively establish non-existence].

If they were indiscriminately identical, then [the reason] could not be absent from all [dissimilar instances]. Since they would thus be mutually conflated, the property to be established (sādhyadharma) would not be fully established.

Second, regarding the establishment of difference: this is intended to establish identity. Therefore, it is established when it is definitely present in similar instances (sapakṣa), and it is excluded when it is entirely absent from dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
"Exclusion" means non-existence; it does not mean that the dissimilar property excludes the similar one. Thus, it is "entirely absent from dissimilar instances."

Thus, the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*) is established. For example, when one says "permanent" in order to prove "impermanent," it is not intended to manifest permanence itself. Third, regarding "sameness and difference":

if the three members [of the syllogism] are established without fault, then that which one has established for oneself will be fully proven; one will be able to refute the opponent's position, and the opponent's position cannot be destroyed.
△ Second, the section on the dual interrogation and specific explanation, which is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of "similar characteristics" (*sādharmya*).

What are called the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)? That which possesses the same meaning as the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is called the similar instance.
For example, when "impermanence" is established, a jar and so forth are the similar instances because they are impermanent.
What is the double interrogation at the end? It refers to the specific explanation provided below. That which is established as the thesis (*pakṣa*) is the "thesis" itself.
That which possesses a logical nature similar to the thesis being established is called the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*).

This is explained by providing an example for the establishment, such as when the thesis of impermanence is established with "being produced" as the reason (*hetu*) and "a jar" and so forth as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore...

This is called the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*). Although this explicitly presents the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it implicitly indicates the logical reason (*hetu*). △ Second, the explanation of the "dissimilar class" (*vipakṣa*).

The dissimilar class refers to those instances where that which is to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is absent. For example, if something were eternal, one would observe that it is not a product, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
The "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*) is that which is different from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). This refers to the explanation of the meaning of "difference" provided below.

It is called "different" because it lacks the same property as that which is to be established in a different location. If one were to establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate this difference, it would be stated: "If there is a phenomenon that is permanent..."
Because the cause is not something produced, it is like empty space; thus, all three members [of the syllogism] differ from the [probandum’s] identity.

Therefore, there can be no identity with the thesis (*sādhya*). Nāgārjuna said: "One should prove its permanence by means of its being unproduced, or establish its being produced by means of its impermanence.
This is precisely that meaning. △ Third, the explanation of the pervasive characteristic (*vyāpti*).

In this context, the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), or the property of being originated by uninterrupted effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), is a property that pervades the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Its necessary presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its universal absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) constitute the reasons for [proving] impermanence and so forth.
This explains the characteristic of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of the reason of impermanence within the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

Here, regarding the reasons within the similar class—namely, among the two reasons such as "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth—if one obtains either of these reasons, it is entirely impermanent; thus, the reason pervades the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

Therefore, it is said that "it is pervasively the property of the subject. The passage beginning with "In the similar [class]" clarifies the sense that the reason of being produced is a property of the subject. This is because...
Because it is present in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and entirely absent from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is established as a reason for impermanence.

Thus, Nāgārjuna stated: "By virtue of being produced, one can establish impermanence. He further said: "The word 'reason' (*hetu*) is spoken in order to manifest the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) within that which is to be inferred;
because it can manifest the thesis (*pakṣa*), it can establish the thesis. However, regarding the aforementioned reason...
Nature is of two kinds: namely, the productive cause (*janakahetu*) and the revealing cause (*vyañjakahetu*). The productive cause is like a seed producing a sprout;

the revealing cause is like a lamp illuminating an object. Each of these has three types. As for the three types of the productive cause: first, the verbal productive cause; second, the cognitive productive cause.

The three causes for the arising of meaning (*artha*). Regarding the three causes for manifestation (*vyañjana-hetu*): first, the cause for manifestation through wisdom; second, the cause for manifestation through speech;

third, the cause for manifestation through meaning. These are explained in detail as set forth in the *Nāgārjuna-śāstra*. △ Third, the section explaining the metaphors, which is divided into two parts. First, stating the number and listing them.
There are two kinds of analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*): first, the analogy of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), and second, the analogy of difference (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

An "analogy" means to bring about understanding through comparison; that is, by using a proximate matter as a point of comparison, one causes [the listener] to attain clear comprehension of the profound Dharma.
Thus, the *Vajraśāstra* states: "An analogy is the meaning of seeing a limit," meaning that by means of a limit already seen, [one understands] what has not yet been seen.
The correct explanation of the conjunction of the seen and the unseen is called an "analogy" (*dṛṣṭānta*). The commentary states:
"The 'seen side' refers to the manifested portion; the 'unseen side' refers to the unmanifested portion. By means of the manifested portion, one clarifies the unmanifested portion."
To ensure that the meaning is consistent, all correct explanations are termed "establishing examples" (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the terms "similar" (*sādharmya*) and "dissimilar" (*vaidharmya*):

these refer to "properties" (*dharma*) when occurring in the context of the reason (*hetu*), whereas they refer to "examples" (*dṛṣṭānta*) when occurring in the context of the illustration. An example is called "similar" when its properties are identical to those of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the subject (*dharmin*);
the "dissimilar" is the opposite of this. Furthermore, an example possesses both an essence (*svabhāva*) and a basis (*āśraya*); for instance, a "jar" serves as the basis. This is because...
The meaning of "impermanence" is established; that which realizes the thesis of impermanence is designated as its "essence. All subsequent instances follow this pattern.
△ Second, the detailed explanation according to the headings, divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The "similar instance" (sapakṣa) is that wherein it is demonstrated that the reason is definitely present; that is to say, if something is produced, one observes it to be impermanent, such as a jar and the like.
"Similarity of property" (*sādharmya*) means that the example cited shares the same properties as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*); therefore, it is called "similar.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the meaning of similarity: it refers to the sharing of the same property as the reason within the example, thereby establishing the certainty of existence.

That is to say, the formal inference (*prayoga*) is established to demonstrate this similarity: taking "being produced" as the reason and "impermanence" as the thesis, with a jar and so forth as the example.

This serves as an analogy. Because the three members [of the syllogism] are perfectly consistent, it is said that they are "similar" (*sādharmya*). △ Second, the explanation of the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya*). Regarding the "dissimilar" (*vaidharmya*):
it is where, in a given case, the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is stated to be absent, and the reason (*hetu*) is universally non-existent there.

That is to say: "If something were eternal, one would see that it is not produced, such as space, etc. Herein, the word "eternal" indicates the absence of impermanence; the phrase "not produced" indicates...
There is nothing to be done. That which exists as non-existent is called "non-existent.

Regarding "dissimilar instance" (*vaidharmya*): it is that which differs from the similar instance (*sādharmya*). If one explains the meaning of "dissimilar" below, it means that at the locus of the example, the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is absent;

while the reason (*hetu*) is stated in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is entirely absent in the dissimilar class. Therefore, it is called a "dissimilar instance. This refers to the formulation of the syllogism (*prayoga*) as follows:

This clarifies the distinction. Here, the subsequent restatement of the distinct meaning serves to demonstrate that there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*).
"In this context" refers to within the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). "Permanent is not impermanent" means there is no similar thesis;

"not produced is unconditioned" means there is no similar reason. As in the example provided below, which uses the case of space to clarify that it is not like a jar and so forth—this is the dissimilar illustration (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).
The expression "like space" indicates that it is not a jar or the like; it is like saying "not existent" in contrast to "existent," which means it is not existent.

Since there is no commonality with dissimilar phenomena (*vijātīya*), the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*) is fully accomplished, thereby avoiding the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). △ Second, the summary of the proof (*sādhana*).
The reasons for the thesis and so forth have already been explained. When such a collection of words is used to enlighten another, it is called the "proof" (*sādhana*).

For example, the statement "Sound is impermanent" is the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*). The statement "Because it is a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

The statement "If something is a product, it is seen to be impermanent, like a jar and so forth" is the statement of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). [The statement] "If it were eternal, it would not be a product... [is the statement of the dissimilar instance].
"To act as if it were like space" refers to the avoidance of verbal expression; these three factors alone are called the "proof" (*sādhana*).

The preceding section has already explained this in detail as a summary in response to what was stated below. Since it was previously indicated that "the collection of statements such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) is called the proof," and this has now been extensively explained above, this serves as a summary.
From the words "as previously stated" onwards, the preceding three factors are summarized to clarify [the point].
The "able to establish" (*sādhana*) is that which is already established. "Far removed from words" means that within the dissimilar (*vipakṣa*), there is no commonality with the thesis (*sādhya*);

thus, by being far removed from the three properties such as impermanence, the property to be established is fully established. The first section concludes. △ Second, the section on fallacious *sādhanas*, divided into three parts.
First, clarifying the faults of the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*), divided into three. First, stating the thesis and enumerating the faults.
Although it may appear to be successfully established, because it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, it is termed a "pseudo-thesis" (*pratijñābhāsa*).

These are: contradiction with direct perception, contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), contradiction with one's own scriptures (*āgama*), contradiction with worldly consensus, contradiction with one's own words, non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-asiddha*), non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣya-asiddha*), non-establishment of both, and that which is already established by common consent (*prasiddha-samāna*).

This clarifies the fallacies that resemble the thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*). Although the "fallacies resembling the thesis" are first indicated below [in the section on] "Desire," the refutations are listed below under "Manifest Perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

This is because if there is any contradiction among the five types of valid cognition, such as manifest perception, then the establishment of the property (*dharma*) is not accomplished; this applies to all four categories, beginning with the "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Because the preceding and succeeding propositions involve a lack of consensus between the proponent and the opponent, the meaning [of the argument] is likewise not established.
△ Second, the detailed explanation according to the headings is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of contradiction (*viruddha*).
Among these, that which contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is, for example, to say that "sound is not audible.

This constitutes a fallacy of the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*). Regarding the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), when they are confronted by the five sense faculties, they are apprehended directly and clearly without depending on verbal designations or conceptual deliberation;
this is called direct perception. A contradiction occurs when the thesis contradicts such direct perception.
It is as stated below, where examples are raised to clarify the fault; hereafter, whenever the term "like" (如) is used, it should be understood according to this principle.
Now, sound is that which is heard by the ear. Since you take "that which is not heard" as your thesis, does this not contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
Contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*) is, for example, to say that a jar and so forth are permanent.
"Inference" refers to measuring by means of comparison, such as inferring fire from seeing smoke. "Contradiction" means that the thesis contradicts inference.
However, since a jar is a produced thing, it is inherently impermanent; yet, having asserted it to be permanent, it contradicts inferential measurement.
If it were not attached [to the object], it would contradict inference (*anumāna*).
As for contradiction with one's own teaching (*svaśāstravirodha*):

for example, the Vaiśeṣika masters establish sound as eternal, whereas the teachings of the Vātsīputrīyas establish it as non-eternal. Now, if one establishes sound as eternal upon the locus (*dharmin*) of sound, then...
This contradicts their own doctrine. The Vaiśeṣikas—that is, the Vātsīputrīyas—are proponents of non-existence;
yet, while maintaining non-existence, they also hold that sound is eternal. Is this not a contradiction of their own doctrine?
Contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka-viruddha*) refers, for example, to saying that the hare-marked [moon] is not the moon because it does not exist as such;
or, for example, saying that human skull-bone is pure because it is a part of a sentient being, just like a conch shell.
That the hare is contained within the moon is what the world universally knows; yet now you say that the hare is not there because of the moon.
Furthermore, that the cranial bone is impure is also what the world universally knows; yet now you say that a human’s cranial bone is pure, like a conch shell.
Both of these statements contradict common worldly understanding.
Regarding contradiction with one's own words: it is like saying, "My mother is a barren woman.
This contradicts one's own words. One who nurtures and raises me is my mother; a barren woman lacks the capacity to nurture and raise, and thus is not truly my mother.
To say, "My mother is a barren woman," is this not a contradiction of one's own words?
How contradictory! △ Second, the explanation of non-establishment.
Regarding "the qualifier not being established": for example, when a follower of the Buddha establishes the destruction of sound against a Sāṃkhya teacher.
The "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) refers to the predicate of the thesis, namely "perishability.

"Not universally established" (*asiddha*) means that when a Buddhist disciple posits the thesis of perishability with respect to the subject "sound" against a proponent of eternalism, the latter does not accept this thesis;
therefore, it is said that the qualifier is not universally established. The Sāṃkhya (Sāṃkhya) are those who maintain the doctrine of permanence. [The opponent] asks for the underlying principle.

"One should refute permanence by means of disintegration and destruction. Why, then, would one incur this fault? Master Xuanzang replied: "In establishing an inference (*anumāna*), there are three types:

those based on oneself, those based on others, and those common to both. Each has its respective qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) according to what is appropriate. If it is an inference based on oneself, it is qualified by the phrase 'admitted by oneself' (*svābhyupagama*).

If it is an inference based on others, it is qualified by the phrase 'you maintain' (*tvad-abhyupagama*). If it is a common inference, it is qualified by the phrase 'ultimate reality' (*paramārtha*). Now, [in this case], we establish..."

Such a person, when later presenting their argument, is unable to rely on what they themselves have established; instead, they resort to indirect phrasing to evade criticism and attempt to cause others to understand.
Therefore, they incur this fault. The *Da chao* states: "‘Self’ refers to one’s own established thesis, intended to cause others to understand it.

For example, the Sarvāstivāda school establishes the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and formulates its own syllogism, saying: ‘My non-informative matter is certainly a real substance of matter.’"

Because the nature of form (*rūpa*) is admitted, just as form and sound are admitted. "By another" means that within the thesis established for another, one points out faults in the proposition (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*);

for example, when refuting the Sarvāstivāda school from the perspective of the Mahāyāna: "Your unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is not a determinate, real form, because you admit it is non-resistant (*apratigha*), like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
"In common" means that within the thesis established for another, one points out a fault in the inference (*anumāna*).

Regarding "the subject of the proposition not being established" (*viśeṣya-asiddha*): for example, when a Sāṃkhya teacher addresses a follower of the Buddha and says, "The self (*ātman*) is volition (*cetanā*).
Here, the "subject of the proposition" (*viśeṣya*) refers to the "divine self" (*pūrvapakṣa-ātman*) mentioned previously.

It is "not established" because while this teacher asserts that the divine self is volition, the internal teaching (Buddhism) does not accept such a divine self; hence it is called "the subject of the proposition not being established. — Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty.

The inference for the establishment of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is stated as follows: "It is necessarily not separate from visual consciousness" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). This is the well-established predicate (*viśeṣya*).
This refers to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the latter member of the proposition as the predicate. Furthermore, it is said:

"The Mahāyāna asserts that the Buddha possesses uncontaminated form (*anāsravarūpa*), while the Hīnayāna asserts that the Buddha possesses contaminated form (*sāsravarūpa*). If these two types of form were established as being consciousness-only, then there would be no common ground between the two parties."

Granted. This would then constitute a fallacy of "non-establishment of the particular" (*viśeṣāprasiddhi*) for both oneself and the other, referring to the subject (*dharmin*) presented in the thesis as the "particularized" (*viśeṣya*).
Recently, some have claimed that when a Buddhist does not accept a tenet established by a non-Buddhist, it is called "non-establishment of the particularizer" (*viśeṣaṇāprasiddhi*);
whereas when a non-Buddhist does not accept a tenet established by a Buddhist, it is called "non-establishment of the particularized. [This distinction is incorrect.]
This is an error.

Regarding "neither being established for both parties": it is like the Vaiśeṣika teacher who, when addressing a follower of the Buddha, posits the self (*ātman*) as the cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
This clarifies that both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are not universally established (*aprasiddha*).

That is to say, when the Vaiśeṣika masters establish the thesis (*pakṣa*) that "inherence" (*samavāya*) is the causal condition for the self (*ātman*) as a substratum (*dharmin*), the internal teachings (Buddhism) do not accept this at all. Therefore, it is said that both are not universally established.
For if one takes the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) as the "self," it is not a truly permanent self; thus, the distinct property (*viśeṣya*) is not established.
If one takes the "self" as the cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), this is not the meaning of the correct causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) taught by the Buddha;
thus, the subject (*dharmin*) is not established.
Regarding "concordant established consensus" (*sādharmya-siddha*): it is as when one says, "Sound is that which is heard. Master Xuanzang stated:
"To support [the opponent's] marks constitutes the fault of supporting their school. Now, regarding the term "concordant" (*fu*):

it refers to when a proponent establishes the thesis that "sound is that which is heard" upon the subject (*dharmin*) of sound; intending to distinguish this from and establish his own school’s doctrine, he instead—[contradicts it].
Because these [positions] correspond, they are called "mutually established correspondence" (*samasiddha*). △ Third, concluding the refutation and returning to the fundamental tenet:
Such manifold words are for the purpose of negating the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; because they cannot establish [anything], and because their formulation is fruitless.
This is called the fallacy of "resembling the thesis" (*pratijñā-sadṛśa*).

This concludes the discussion on the nine fallacies mentioned previously, returning to the core point. Now, in establishing an inference (*anumāna*), one must first employ wisdom to comprehend the causes of all phenomena;
thus, whatever inference is established will not contradict its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) will necessarily be proven, and the result will necessarily follow.
There is. Now, this which is proposed contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth;

since it contradicts the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established, and because there is no result, it is called a "pseudo-thesis" (*pratijñābhāsa*). "To negate" means to contradict the meaning.

"Not admitting establishment" refers to the fact that among the nine [types of fallacies] mentioned previously, if there is even one contradiction, then establishment is not admitted. This is "establishing without result."
This means that once the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established, there can be no result. △ Second, the explanation of the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), divided into two parts.
First, following the previous section, the subsequent is indicated:

"The fallacious theses have already been explained; now the fallacious reasons shall be explained. The unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*)—these are called fallacious reasons."
This refers back to the previous general definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). A "fallacious reason" is so called because it contradicts that which is to be established (*sādhya*).
Thus, the *Upāyahṛdaya* states: "A fallacious reason is like a mirage appearing as water, yet being actually not water;
if a proponent, through the embellishment of their speech, treats it as water, this is called a fallacious reason. II. Detailed Explanation According to the Definition.

This is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of "non-establishment" (asiddha) is divided into two. First, the general enumeration of the categories: there are four types of non-establishment:

first, non-establishment for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*); second, non-establishment for one of the parties (*anyatarāsiddha*); third, non-establishment through doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*); and fourth, non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

The four types of non-establishment [of the reason] are as follows: first, the reason is not admitted as certain by either the proponent or the opponent regarding the thesis; second, it is not admitted solely by the opponent;
third, the reason is subject to doubt and indecision regarding the thesis; and fourth, one conceives of space as being substantially existent.

Regarding the argument against those who deny emptiness, the locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished; these are all fallacies of non-establishment. △ Second, the specific explanation of the meaning of these fallacies:
For example, in establishing that sound is impermanent and so forth, if one were to say, "Because it has the nature of being visible to the eye," this would be unestablished for both parties.

"Non-establishment for both parties" refers to a probans (*hetu*) that is not accepted by either the proponent or the opponent, while being pervasive across the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*).

For example, if one were to establish "impermanence" as the thesis (*pakṣa*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) "sound," and use "the nature of being visible to the eye" as the reason (*hetu*), this would be unaccepted by both sides and is thus termed "non-establishment for both.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "That which is not accepted by both [parties] is certainly not a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). As it is said:
There is [the following argument]: "Sound is impermanent because it is visible to the eye, and because it is a product.
Against the proponent of the theory that sound is manifest (*abhivyakti-vādin*), either one of these reasons is unestablished (*asiddha*).
This statement correctly expresses the reason by abbreviating the thesis (*pakṣa*). To state it fully, it should be: "Just as there is an establishment of the thesis that sound is impermanent..."
[The proponent] always states the reason: "because it is produced by effort" (*kṛtakatvāt*). This reason is accepted only by the proponent himself.

If one argues for the thesis that sound is permanent and employs the reason of being produced, the opponent does not accept it; this is called "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*). Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
Furthermore, regarding opponents who do not grant [the same] consent: for example, in response to the Manifestationist (Śabdika) school, [one argues] "because it is produced.

As for the Manifestationist, the sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The external Śabdika teachers claim that the characteristic of sound is eternal, being neither produced nor destroyed."
However, it is only through being emitted that it becomes manifest; therefore, it is called "manifested by sound.
When doubt arises regarding the nature of mist and the like, what is said is for the purpose of establishing the existence of fire as a combination of the great elements.
Doubt does not establish [the point]. "Fog" is a phenomenon that exists. "Suspicion" refers to suspecting fog to be smoke. "Great elements" (mahābhūta) refers to the four great elements.
It is through the conjunction of the great elements with fire that the characteristic of smoke arises. Because one seeks to establish smoke, an explanation is provided. Now, regarding this...

Taking the nature of mist and the like as the subject, with doubt serving as the "smoke," one might attempt to establish the existence of fire through the conjunction of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

However, such a statement will certainly not produce knowledge in the person; thus, the establishment of the property (*dharma*) fails. Therefore, it is said that "hesitation renders [the reason] unestablished.

For example, if one says "sound is eternal" yet remains indecisive and hesitant, and then establishes "audibility" as the logical reason (*hetu*), one will be unable to resolve whether the thesis (*pakṣa*) is eternal or non-eternal.
This is precisely the meaning of "certainty" (*niścaya*). This section merely clarifies the reason for hesitation; it almost seems unnecessary to formulate a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*). [Thesis:

Space (*ākāśa*) is substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because it is that upon which qualities (*guṇa*) depend. [Against those who argue for non-existent space: The locus of the reason (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is unestablished.
Space is a phenomenon (*dharma*); it possesses a real substratum (*āśraya*). The reason (*hetu*) given is: "because it is that upon which qualities (*guṇa*) depend.

If this reason is confronted with the position that space does not exist, then the substratum is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*). Since space itself does not even exist, what could serve as the substratum for its qualities?
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said: "When confronted [by such an opponent], the existence of space cannot be established; the phenomenon under discussion is unestablished."

This is precisely that meaning. △ Second, the explanation of the inconclusive [reasons] (anaikāntika) is divided into two parts. First, the general enumeration of their number: there are six types of inconclusive reasons.
First, the common (sādhāraṇa); second, the uncommon (asādhāraṇa); third, that which occurs in a portion of the similar class (sapakṣa) but pervades the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);

fourth, that which occurs in a portion of the dissimilar class but pervades the similar class; fifth, that which occurs in a portion of both classes; and sixth, the contradictory decisive (viruddhāvyabhicārin).

Regarding the term "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*): this refers to a reason that, with respect to the thesis (*pakṣa*), cannot be determined as being present in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Because it is contradictory for both the proponent and the opponent regarding the three members of the syllogism, it cannot definitively establish a single thesis;
all such reasons are inconclusive reasons. 2. Specific Explanation of the Meaning of the Fallacies.

Among these, the "common" (sādhāraṇa) [inconclusive reason] is as follows: for example, if one says, "Sound is eternal because it is an object of cognition," this reason is common to both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal;
therefore, it is inconclusive. For instance, is sound impermanent because it is an object of cognition like a jar, or is it eternal like space?
Because it is an object of cognition, sound is eternal.
Regarding the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), it means that a single probans is shared by two theses (*pakṣa*).

For example, when one establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) below [the thesis], and concludes with the fallacy below "eternal" or "non-eternal," it means that the single probans, "being an object of cognition," can establish both theses, "eternal" and "non-eternal. Since there are these two theses...
If they share a single causal nature, then this single cause lacks determinative power regarding the two propositions; therefore, it is called an "inconclusive reason" (*anaikāntika-hetu*).
This is because, as will be explained below regarding the grounds for inconclusiveness, [the reason] is like a jar and so forth, being a property that is merely an object of cognition (*prameya*).
Sound is impermanent because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), just like space and so forth. [Alternatively,] sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*);
this reason is excluded from both the class of the eternal and the class of the non-eternal. This is what is called the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason].

Because nothing else exists outside of the permanent and the impermanent, this is a reason for doubt (*anaikāntika*). Of what nature is this "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*)? Regarding the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*):
it refers to a state where [the property] exists in neither of the two positions (*pakṣa*), and thus is called unshared.

As stated below in the formal inference (*prayoga*), the fallacy is explained as follows: regarding the permanent, non-production (*akṛtakatva*) is cited as the reason; regarding the impermanent, production (*kṛtakatva*) is cited.

This reason that has been heard serves as the cause. Since this reason is absent in both schools, it is said that they are "all free" from it—not only the categories of permanence and impermanence, but other schools outside of these two are likewise not possessed of the characteristics of this reason.
It is that which establishes certainty. Therefore, it is called the "cause of hesitation. This is the subsequent refutation, which sets forth the reason for the hesitation:
namely, since the nature of this cause is already excluded from both the categories of permanence and impermanence, to what kind of class does it belong?

Regarding that which occurs in one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and occurs throughout the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*): for example, it is said, "Sound is not produced immediately after volitional effort, because it is impermanent.
In this case, the thesis (*pakṣa*)—"not produced immediately after volitional effort"—has lightning, space, and so forth as its similar class.
This property of impermanence exists in lightning and the like, but does not exist in space and the like. [It is] not produced immediately after volitional effort...
Establishing the thesis: taking jars and the like as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), this reason is present throughout them.

Since these reasons—using lightning and jars as the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—are thus indeterminate (*anaikāntika*): [the reason] "because of being produced by effort" is indeterminate because, while jars and the like are impermanent, they are produced by effort;
whereas [the reason] "because of being impermanent" is indeterminate because, while lightning and the like are impermanent, they are not produced by effort.
Now, regarding what is called a "reason" (*hetu*): it must exist pervasively within the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and be entirely absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) to be a valid reason.

In the present case, [the reason] occurs only in a portion of the similar class, yet conversely occurs pervasively in the dissimilar class. Thus, there are places where it does not exist, and places where it is not non-existent;
therefore, it constitutes a fallacy. As stated in the formal proof (*prayoga*) below: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "non-eternality" and so forth are the [predicate].
Thesis: [Sound] is not produced by effort, because its nature is impermanent, like the sound of wind. Herein, the fault is demonstrated below:

if this thesis takes both lightning and space as the corroborative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), then this reason of "impermanence" exists in respect to lightning and the like—since lightning does not abide for even a moment and thus possesses the nature of impermanence—but it does not exist in respect to space and the like.

It abides eternally through emptiness, for it is not impermanent. These two [reasons] function only within a portion of lightning; therefore, they constitute inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika-hetu*).

If this thesis takes a jar or similar object as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then the nature of the reason would be present throughout the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), while its opposite would be present throughout the dissimilar instances.
This is because, in this case, the reason of impermanence applies to both the jar and lightning as things belonging to the same category. Now...
Taking the jar as a dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*), it is indeed confused with the same reason (*sādhana*); therefore, it is also an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*).

As will be explained below regarding the presentation of similar characteristics: since both the jar and lightning are impermanent by nature, "being produced through effort" or "not being produced through effort" constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Although this thesis is free from fault in both the similar and dissimilar classes, this [example] merely points out a fault in the reason. It does not...
The treatise discusses the existence or non-existence of logical fallacies (*dūṣaṇa*).
Regarding that which "occurs in one part of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and occurs pervasively in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*"):

for example, if one establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) stating, "Sound is produced by immediate effort, because it is impermanent," the similar instances for the thesis "produced by immediate effort" are things such as pots. Its...

The nature of impermanence is present throughout this [subject]. Taking lightning, space, and so forth as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it exists in some parts of them—such as lightning—and is absent in others—such as space.
Therefore, as before, this too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

This clarifies the fallacy of being present in only one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). For example, when establishing a formal inference (*prayoga*), one sets forth the reason as "produced by volitional effort" (*kṛtaka*) and then explains the fallacy:

this thesis takes a jar as the similar example (*sapakṣa*), because a jar possesses the nature of impermanence; since the reason is present throughout this [class], it is said to be "pervasive" (*vyāpta*).
However, if lightning and space are taken as the dissimilar examples (*vipakṣa*), then the reason exists in one part—namely, lightning—but in space it is... [absent].

Since this [reason] is non-existent in one part [of the subject], it is said that "one part turns" (ekadeśavṛtti). Therefore, the following section cites the preceding case to conclude the refutation:
namely, because this reason—lightning and the jar—both belong to the same class (sādharmya), it is also inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Regarding "occurrence in one part of both similar and dissimilar instances": for example, when it is said that sound is permanent because it lacks material resistance (*amūrtatva*).

Here, the thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence takes space (*ākāśa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*). The property of lacking material resistance exists in space and so forth, but does not exist in atoms and so forth.
Taking things such as pleasure and space as the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*): [the reason] exists in pleasure and so forth, but does not exist in jars and so forth.
Therefore, because this reason shares the same property with both pleasure and space, it is also called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
In this case, [the reason] occurs in only one part of both the similar and dissimilar examples; therefore, it is called "occurring in one part of both categories" (*ubhayapakṣaikadeśavṛtti*).
It constitutes a fallacy because it contradicts the requirement that [the reason] must be present throughout the similar class and entirely absent from the dissimilar class.

As will be established in the formal syllogism below, the fallacy is analyzed therein as follows: if this thesis of "permanence" takes space and atoms as its two similar examples, then [the reason] is absent in these.
The cause of resistance exists in relation to space and the like, because space is devoid of resistance;
it does not exist in relation to atoms and the like, because atoms possess the nature of resistance. These two [categories] function only with respect to one portion of space.

This constitutes an indeterminate reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*). If one takes the two phenomena of the jar and pleasure as the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then [the reason] exists in pleasure and so forth because pleasure lacks material obstruction (*sapratigha*);
yet it is absent in jars and so forth because jars possess material obstruction.

Since these two [reasons] apply only partially to pleasure, the following concludes the fault: namely, that this reason—whether applied to pleasure or to space—belongs entirely to the same class [as the subject].

Because they share the same nature as phenomena (*dharma*). Since pleasure shares the same nature as emptiness, to now reverse this and treat it as a dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) would mean that the absence [of the probandum] is not pervasive across all dissimilar instances;
thus, it is also an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*).

Regarding the "contradictory certainty" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*): for example, one may establish the thesis that "sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," while another establishes that "sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound.
Since both of these are reasons characterized by doubt, they are both termed "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

Master Xuanzang said: "When two opponents dispute over a single property (*dharma*) that exists, their reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*udāharaṇa*) differ, yet each must possess the three characteristics—namely, presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), and universal concomitance (*vyāpti*).
However, because these [reasons] fail to produce correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) in one another, both parties remain in doubt and cannot definitively establish a single thesis.

This is called the 'inconclusive fallacy of contradictory determination' (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). For example, regarding the property of sound, it is common [to both sides]... [The argument is established].
The measures are distinct. Since they do not mutually produce correct cognition, they constitute the reason of indecisive doubt (*anaikāntika*). Question:

In the case of "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," which serves as a true proof (*sādhana*) to illustrate the correct principle by way of an example, why does this also become an instance of indecisive doubt?
Answer: Whenever one establishes an inference (*anumāna*), the intention is to refute the opponent.
At such times, one must rely on the provisional expressions established by oneself to avoid errors;

thus, one can generate right knowledge in others and definitively establish a school of thought without the fault of being inconclusive. Otherwise, it likewise becomes inconclusive. △ Third, the explanation of contradictory [reasons] is divided into two parts.
First, stating the number and listing the names.

There are four types of contradiction: namely, the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the property (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the property (*dharma-viśeṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), the contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the locus (*dharmin-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*), and the contradictory reason regarding the specific qualification of the locus (*dharmin-viśeṣaṇa-viruddha-hetu*).

Regarding the contradictory [reason]: the reason, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the thesis itself (*pakṣa*), and the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*) all share four faults. II. Detailed explanation according to the headings:
Among these, the "contradictory reason regarding the specific characteristic of the property" (*dharmasvalakṣaṇaviruddhahetu*) is as follows:

for example, to say "Sound is permanent, because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*), or "because it is produced by immediate volitional effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*). This reason exists only in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); therefore, it is contradictory.

The "intrinsic characteristic of the property" (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa*) refers to the intrinsic characteristic of the property that constitutes the predicate (*pakṣadharma*) in the subsequent formulation.

A "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*) refers to a reason that contradicts the intrinsic characteristic of the property. For example, consider the following formal argument (*prayoga*): "Sound is the subject; 'it is necessarily permanent' is the thesis (*pakṣa*);
the reason is 'because it is produced and emitted. Below this, the fault is analyzed: namely, this "produced [nature]"...
The nature [of the subject] is a cause of impermanence; it should exist only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Now, to use this to prove a thesis of permanence is therefore contradictory.
Thus it is said: "Where there is no similar class (*sapakṣa*), the proponent's thesis is not established;
where there is a dissimilar class, the opposite thesis of the opponent is instead established."

Regarding the reason that contradicts the specific qualification of the thesis (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddhahetu*): for example, it is said that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another because they are composite in nature, like bedding and other such things.

While this reason can indeed establish that the eyes and so forth must exist for the sake of another, it likewise establishes the opposite of the specific qualification of the thesis to be proven—that is, it establishes that those composite things which exist for the sake of another, such as bedding, exist for the sake of the composite itself.
Regarding "that which is utilized" (the term *saṃcita* is recorded as *saṃgraha* in some editions),
the distinction of phenomena refers to the specific characteristics intended by the proponent within the subject (*pakṣa*) and the property (*dharma*) presented subsequently.

The contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) refers to a reason that contradicts the specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) of the property to be proven (*dharma*). For example, as stated below in the formal inference (*prayoga*):
"The eye and so forth must exist for the sake of another," because there is the intention [of the proponent] that they are necessarily not for the sake of another—this is the specific qualification.

This reason is then exposed as a fallacy; namely, this reason of being an aggregate (*saṃghāta-hetu*), if it were to establish [the thesis], would necessarily establish that [the eye and so forth] exist for the sake of another.
This immediately contradicts the [proposition] that it "will certainly not be for the sake of another," thereby accomplishing two things with a single stroke. Thus it is said:

"Just as this reason can establish that the eyes and so forth must be for the sake of another, it likewise establishes the contradiction of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
The section beginning with "accumulation" concludes that they must indeed be for the sake of another. According to the *Saptati-śāstra* (The Seventy Verses on Gold), it says:
By my own nature, I know that the conjunction of two factors gives rise to all phenomena and provides them for my enjoyment;
therefore, I know there is a self. Furthermore, a verse asks: "How is it known that there is a self? The answer states: "Because aggregations exist for the sake of another.
The prose commentary explains: "I observe that all aggregations in the world exist for the sake of another, just as, for example, beds, mats, and so forth."

These aggregates are not for one's own use; they are necessarily established for the sake of another. Even the collection of the five great elements is called a "body. This body does not exist for itself;
it is definitively known to be for another. That "other" is precisely the self. Therefore, one knows that the self truly exists.
Based on this, the proponent establishes that the cause of accumulation must be for the use of another; thus, it is certain that [the self] can indeed be established through faith.
Would this not constitute the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristics of the subject (*dharmin*)?

An example of a reason that contradicts the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the subject is as follows: "Existence (*sattā*) is not a substance, not a quality, and not an activity, because it possesses [the universal] 'existence,' and because it possesses qualities and activities, just like the universal 'homogeneity' (*sāmānya-tva*).
This reason, just as it can establish the negation of [being] a substance and so forth, likewise [establishes its own contradictory].
It is also capable of establishing the negation of existence, because both [the reason and the predicate] are determinate.
"The self-characteristic of the subject" (dharmin-svalakṣaṇa) refers to the self-characteristic of the subject as it was previously stated.

A "contradictory reason" (viruddha-hetu) means that the reason contradicts the self-characteristic of the subject. For example, to establish this, one sets forth the following formal argument: "Existence exists."

[The opponent claims: "Dharma (the universal) is not a real substance, quality, or action; therefore, it is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it possesses real substance, quality, and action.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: 'just like the nature of similarity and difference (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). As for 'possessing the nature,' this refers to the 'Great Existence' (*mahāsattā*) among the six categories. The *Daochao* states:
'Because substance, quality, and action are all equally possessed of existence (*sattā*), there exists a separate dharma as their essence apart from substance, quality, and action. Based on this..."
"Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*). It is so called because it possesses reality (*sattva*) and so forth. However, based on this nature of Great Existence, it is said to encompass two meanings:

the three categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karma*) are identical with the nature of existence. Because of this Great Existence, substance and the others possess existence;

this is precisely the nature of being an object of cognition (*ālambana*) that does not depart from substance, quality, and activity. Because it takes substance, quality, and activity as its objects, it is named "having objects" (*sālambana*). [It is] distinct from...
Apart from substance, quality, and action, there exists a distinct dharma as its essence; this is precisely the nature of non-existence that is distinct from substance, quality, and action.
By clearly discerning within this the natures of existence and non-existence, the distinctions between their respective characteristics become evident.
As for the nature of generality and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), it also possesses a distinct real entity apart from substance and the others; therefore, it is taken as an analogy.
This reason, based on its essential nature (*svabhāva*), serves as a counter-illustration of contradiction.

That is to say, just as this reason—such as "having reality" (*sattva*)—is able to establish the negation of [the property of] having reality and so forth, it should likewise be able to establish the negation of the subject (*dharmin*) that possesses existence.

Now, since it cannot establish the negation of having reality and so forth, it necessarily cannot establish the negation of existence; thus, it constitutes a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject.

This is an error. "Negation" (遮) means "non-existence" (非). Regarding "both being determinate": this refers to the fact that if something can establish a thesis (*pakṣa*), it can also establish existence, because their essence depends on the same [substratum].
As for the "six categories" (*ṣatpadārtha*), they are the constructs of the Vaiśeṣika masters: namely, first, substance (*dravya*) has nine kinds;
second, quality (*guṇa*) has twenty-four kinds; third, action (*karman*) has five kinds; and fourth, generality (*sāmānya*) has only one kind.
The five types of identity and difference constitute a single category, as do the six types of conjunction; these are all explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śata-śāstra*.

Regarding the "reason that contradicts a specific attribute of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha-hetu*), it is, for example, this very reason [previously cited] with respect to a specific attribute of the subject within the aforementioned thesis.

It establishes the nature of having a real object (*sālambanatva*), and is likewise able to establish its opposite, the nature of not having a real object (*anālambanatva*), just as in the case of negating [the existence of] substances (*dravya*) and so forth, because both are definitively established.
Regarding the qualification of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣaṇa*): it refers to the specific characteristic intended by the proponent regarding the subject presented in the thesis (*pūrvapakṣa*).
