Because there is a distinction between having an objective basis (*sālambanatva*) and not having an objective basis (*anālambanatva*), the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) refers to a reason that contradicts a specific qualification of the subject (*dharmin*).

"As in this very reason" means, for example, as in the case where the very reason—such as "being a single real entity, a quality, and so forth"—is applied to the aforementioned subject as a qualification, namely, as having an objective basis. This [reason] lacks establishment (*asiddha*).

Regarding the text on formal inference (*pramāṇa*), one should formulate the inference as follows: "Existence (*sattā*) is the subject (*dharmin*); it is not separate from substance, quality, and action;
this is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it possesses one substance,' and 'because it possesses qualities and actions.

This also establishes the fault of contradicting the specific characteristics of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*) explained below. That is to say, just as this reason can establish that existence has conditions (*sālambanatva*), it also..."

The capacity to establish [an object] is contradictory with the nature of having an object (*sālambanatva*); to function as that which lacks an object is precisely what constitutes the nature of lacking an object.
This is a contradiction of the specific characteristics of this very nature of having an object, because it negates both [the categories of] "real" (*dravya*) and so forth as being determinate.

As the Tripiṭaka Master established the inference for consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-anumāna*), he said: "Form is definitely separated from visual consciousness; form is definitely not separated from visual consciousness."

This constitutes a fallacy regarding the qualification of the thesis (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*). Since the three scriptural baskets (*tripiṭaka*) establish that meditative concentration is not separated from visual consciousness and visible forms, it contradicts the [opponent's] claim that concentration is separated from visual consciousness and visible forms;
thus, there is the fallacy of contradicting the qualification of the thesis. △ Third, the section on the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), divided into two parts.
First, following the preceding [section], the subsequent [part] is introduced.

The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) have already been explained; now the fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) shall be discussed. There are five types of fallacious similar examples (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*):

first, the unestablishedness of the probans (*sādhanadharma-asiddha*); second, the unestablishedness of the probandum (*sādhyadharma-asiddha*); third, the unestablishedness of both; fourth, the lack of connection (*anupanaya*); and fifth, the inverted connection (*viparītopanaya*).

There are likewise five types of fallacious dissimilar examples (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): first, the failure to exclude the probandum (*sādhyāvyāvṛtta*); second, the failure to exclude the probans (*sādhanāvyāvṛtta*); and third, the failure to exclude both.
"Four types of non-separation; five types of inverted separation.

This refers back to the previous general indication of fallacies regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). "That which resembles a similar example" (*sādharmya-sama*) means that the example established is not identical to the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), or the property (*dharma*);
therefore, it is called "resembling. This is because a similar example is intended to demonstrate that the reason is invariably present within the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

There is the nature of existence. Since these are now not identical, one cannot definitively establish its existence; thus, the fallacy of "sameness" (sādharmya-sama) is incurred. Regarding what is called a "fallacious dissimilarity" (vaidharmya-sama):

this refers to a case where the example provided in the proof is not distinct from the property of the thesis or the reason; hence it is named "fallacious dissimilarity. This is because a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) ought to lack the property to be established that exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*);
since it does not lack it here, the fallacy of "dissimilarity" (vaidharmya-sama) is incurred. The fallacies of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and "separation" (*viyoga*) are found in the text.

Regarding "the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) being unestablished": for example, it is said that sound is permanent because it lacks material obstruction (*amūrtatva*). [In this case,] one observes that all things lacking material obstruction...

This is permanent, just like an atom (*paramāṇu*). However, regarding that atom, while the property to be established—namely, permanence—exists, the establishing property—namely, lack of material obstruction (*sapratighatva*)—does not exist, because all atoms possess the nature of material obstruction.

This analogy cannot establish the reason (*hetu*). That is to say, while the analogy of a material atom (*paramāṇu*) may establish the thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence, it does not establish the nature of the probans (*sādhana*) as being unimpeded;
therefore, it is said that "the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished.

As stated below in the formal inference (*prayoga*), the phrase "all those that are... [is the application]. However, the passage beginning with "but that... sets forth the reason why it is unestablished, namely: this...
This is analogous to establishing the thesis that "eternality exists" because these atoms possess an eternal nature;
yet, regarding the probans, "the absence of material resistance," it is non-existent because these atoms do possess material resistance.
Regarding the non-establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*): this refers to the statement that "like cognition.

For while the property used as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*)—namely, the existence of something without material obstruction—is established, the property to be proven—namely, permanence—is absent, because all cognitions are impermanent.

This analogy cannot establish the thesis (*pakṣa*). That is to say, the analogy of the cognition of impermanence merely establishes the probans (*sādhana*) of "lack of material resistance" (*apratighatva*), but it does not establish the probandum (*sādhya*) of the thesis of permanence; therefore, it is said that "the property to be established is unestablished.

This case possesses only the analogy while lacking the thesis and the reason, as can be understood by comparison with what preceded. However, the passage beginning with "all... provides the reason why it is unestablished: namely, this cognition...
This is analogous to the reason (*hetu*) "being non-obstructive" [proving] "existence": because this cognizing mind lacks physical form, it is established that its nature is eternal;
yet because this cognizing mind undergoes momentary transition and change, its nature is impermanent. Thus, regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established, its permanence is non-existent.
Regarding the case where both are unestablished, there are further two types: existence and non-existence. If one says "like a jar," both existents are unestablished.
If one speaks of "like space" in response to a discourse on non-existence, both non-existents are unestablished.

This clarifies that both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are unestablished. There are two types: existence and non-existence. "Existence" refers to using the aforementioned thesis and reason, as in the statement:
"Sound is eternal, because it lacks material resistance. "Non-existence" refers to the opposite of the aforementioned thesis and reason, as in the statement:
"Sound is impermanent, because it possesses material resistance. Thus, one takes the thesis of eternity as existence, and the thesis of impermanence [as non-existence].

This is because [the example] does not exist. To explain the fault in the following statement: if one argues against the thesis of "permanence" using a jar as the example, then both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are unestablished (*asiddha*).
This is because a jar is impermanent and possesses material obstruction; therefore, it is said that there is a failure of both.
If, however, one argues against the thesis of "impermanence" using space (*ākāśa*) as the example, then both the thesis and the reason are likewise unestablished, because space—[is permanent...]
Because their nature is eternally devoid of substantial obstruction, it is said that neither [the reason nor the thesis] is unestablished.

"Lacking conjunction" means that there is no actual union at this location; rather, both the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) appear together in relation to things such as a jar, just as one says:
"In a jar, one perceives both the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*)."
Regarding the term "lack of application" (*anupanaya*): it refers to not stating the word of application within the formal inference (*pramāṇa*).

Generally, when establishing an inference, one ought to state the words of application, such as: "Whatever is produced is impermanent," and so forth. Since those words are now missing, this fault is incurred.
This point is the same as the locus of the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). However, the reason for the lack of application is set forth below, namely:
However, in the case of [the example of] a jar and so forth, there is no proper coordination between the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*).
For instance, when one says "that which is produced below appears as a pair," this refers to an inverted application (*viparīta-yojanā*). That is to say, one should state:
"Whatever is produced is impermanent," yet one instead states in reverse: "Whatever is impermanent is produced."
This constitutes a "reversed application" (*viparīta-upanaya*), which consists of stating the combined terms in a reversed order relative to the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

A "correct application" (*samyag-upanaya*) is defined as placing the reason (*hetu*) first and the thesis (*pakṣa*) last; for example: "Sound is the subject (*dharmin*); 'impermanence' is the thesis (*sādhya*); the reason is 'because it is produced' (*kṛtakatvāt*);
the application states: 'Whatever is produced is impermanent'; the example states: 'just like a jar, etc. Now, the present application is the reverse of this.
Therefore, this fault is established. △ Next, the conclusion reiterates the commonality of the method.

△ Second, the explanation of the heterogeneous [example] is divided into two parts. First, the specific clarification of the heterogeneous fallacies.

Regarding the case where that which is established in the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*) is not excluded: for example, suppose someone says, "Whatever is impermanent is seen to possess resistance, like an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Because the atom is established as having the property of permanence, the property of permanence [in the subject] is not excluded; thus, the probans (the property of possessing resistance) is absent in the atom.
Therefore, the property to be proven (impermanence) is absent. This constitutes a fallacy of the "unestablished reason" (*asiddha-hetu*).

This clarifies that the counter-example (dṛṣṭānta) cannot refute the thesis (*pakṣa*). For within the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), there ought to be a universal absence of the property in question;

yet here, the dissimilar example possesses the same property as that which is to be established. Therefore, it is said that it does not refute [the thesis]. Furthermore, regarding the preceding similar instance where the thesis was "eternal" and the reason was "lacking material resistance," one should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Sound is impermanent, because it has the nature of material resistance. Within the dissimilar cases, one excludes [the reason] by saying: all...
Regarding "impermanence": one perceives that [the subject] possesses resistance, just like an atom (*paramāṇu*). This merely refutes the reason (*hetu*) but does not refute the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Because it is stated below that there is no refutation of the [thesis], and since the atom is permanent, it cannot refute that permanent thesis;
however, because the atom possesses resistance, it can refute that reason of being without resistance.
Regarding "not refuting the probans": this refers to stating that it is like [the case of] karma; one merely refutes the probandum (sādhyadharma) without refuting the probans (sādhanadharma).
For they assert that all karmas lack material resistance (*sapratigha*).
This merely refutes the thesis (*pakṣa*) but does not refute the reason (*hetu*). Because this analogy of "action" (*karman*) is impermanent, it can refute the thesis of permanence;

however, because it lacks material obstruction (*sapratighatva*), it cannot refute the reason. This [passage] presents the analogy alone; the thesis and reason are to be understood according to what precedes.
The subsequent explanation clarifies the grounds for why it does not refute [the reason].
Regarding "neither being negated": this refers to the proponents of existence (*astivādin*). It is said to be like space;
for space does not negate its own nature of permanence or its nature of non-obstruction, because space is described as being permanent and non-obstructive.

This clarifies that neither the thesis (*pakṣa*) nor the reason (*hetu*) is negated. "That which exists" refers to the permanent lack of material obstruction within the class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

"Like space" specifically points to the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). The phrase "by that" and below correctly clarifies the non-negation; the phrase "because it is said" and below sets forth the grounds for this non-negation.
"Non-separation" means, for example, stating that a jar possesses the nature of impermanence and the nature of resistance.

It is called "non-separation" because no term of separation is expressed regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) are presented together with respect to the jar.
However, it has not been stated that all impermanent things are seen to possess material obstruction, such as jars and the like; therefore, this fallacy arises.
As for "reversing the separation," it refers to stating, for example: "All things possessing material obstruction are impermanent."
"Reversal" (*viparyāsa*) refers to stating the words of separation (*vyatireka*) in reverse order. If stated correctly, it should say:

"Whatever is impermanent is seen to possess resistance," placing the thesis (*pakṣa*) first and the reason (*hetu*) afterwards; this would constitute a correct statement. Since the present case is the opposite of this, it is called "reversal.

This constitutes the ten faults regarding similarity and dissimilarity within the pseudo-example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*); the first three all clarify faults pertaining to the thesis and the reason. The latter...

The first two [cases] clarify only the faults of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*). As for the first three clarifying the faults regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*):

because while the thesis and the reason are both consistent, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is inconsistent, this results in the uncertainty of its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the uncertainty of its absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

Why is it that when [the reason] is stated to be present in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), and when it is stated to be absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is called "separation" (*viyoga*)? Answer: Because it must be definitely present in the similar class; where there is presence, there is conjunction, and conjunction is precisely establishment (*siddhi*).

In the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), [the reason] must be entirely absent; its absence constitutes its exclusion, and exclusion is precisely what is meant by "separation" (*viyoga*). △ Finally, the summary of the fallacies of formulation:

The second section, the gate of that which resembles the means of proof, is concluded. △ Third, the section on true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is divided into two parts. First, the general presentation of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
Furthermore, for the sake of one's own awakening, it should be known that there are only two means of valid cognition: direct perception and inference (*anumāna*).
This clarifies that the two types of wisdom—direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—lead solely to one's own awakening.

This is because direct wisdom can penetrate the non-arising of phenomena, while inferential wisdom can know the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions; thus, within the process of establishing [theses] and refuting [oppositions], one remains free from all faults.

The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "True wisdom universally knows the gate of the true suchness of the mind; conventional wisdom universally knows the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind."
The differentiation of dependent origination is itself self-awakening. △ Second, the specific explanation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Herein, "direct perception" refers to non-conceptualization. If there is correct cognition regarding objects such as form, it is free from all conceptualizations, such as names and categories;
because it functions distinctly for each manifest object, it is called direct perception.
Within this context, it refers to the true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) wisdom of self-awakening; it is the correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) that establishes and refutes in accordance with reality.

This means that by means of this wisdom, one realizes the non-arising of all phenomena and realizes the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas; therefore, within the process of establishing and refuting, one remains free from all faults.
"Direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifest appearance; "perception" (*pramāṇa*) is defined as the standard of certainty, which is to say, to illuminate what is manifest through direct wisdom.

Regarding the object (*ālambana*): it functions with respect to its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), being certain and free from error. It directly attains the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and is devoid of all conceptualization;

thus, it is called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*). If one were to provide a lower-level explanation: this non-conceptual wisdom, in relation to objects such as form (*rūpa*), does not carry linguistic designations (*nāman*) and lacks a deliberative mind (*parīkṣaka-citta*).
Therefore, it is said to be "free from all conceptualizations," such as names and categories (*nāma-jāti-ādi-vikalpa*). It does not take as its objective support that which is hidden (*gūḍha*).

Because it is not obscured or separated by darkness, nor by objects of the past or future, it is called "manifestly manifest. It realizes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object, unlike the six consciousnesses which take common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as their objects;
thus it is said to "function separately in each manifestation. Because it functions within the sphere of specific characteristics, it is termed "true direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
This has many varieties, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts. IV. True Inference (*anumāna*) is divided into two parts.
First, the individual explanation of inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the term "inference," it refers to observing an object by means of its various characteristics (*liṅga*). There are three types of characteristics, as previously explained.

With that as its cause, there arises a correct cognition regarding the object of inference, such as the knowledge that "there is fire" or "it is impermanent," and this is called inference (*anumāna*).
"Comparison" (upamāna) refers to drawing an analogy; "inference" (anumāna) refers to measurement. For example, when one sees smoke across a mountain, one necessarily knows it is fire;

although one has not seen it directly, it is not erroneous. This is because one first establishes the fundamental cause of all phenomena through direct realization, and only thereafter does one formulate the inference.

"Various characteristics" (*liṅga*) refers to the three characteristics [of the reason] within the causal stage. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the meaning of the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Threefold" refers to its pervading the three aspects—homogeneity, heterogeneity, and the entire domain.
Because these three characteristics serve as the reason, they cause correct knowledge to arise in the listener regarding the object of inference, such that they comprehend impermanence and so forth;
therefore, it is called inference (*anumāna*). △ Second, the summary of the two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Within the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is precisely cognition that is called the "result" (*phala*), because it is the characteristic of realization and because it manifests as having an operative function;
it is also termed a "means of valid cognition.

Thus, cognition itself is called the result—referring specifically to the result of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the result of inference (*anumāna*)—and there is no separate result apart from these.
Why is this? Because wisdom is the characteristic of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-lakṣaṇa*), wisdom is itself the fruit. Regarding the "characteristic of realization":

direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) wisdom is able to realize and know the non-differentiated realm; true inference (*anumāna*) wisdom is able to realize and know the realm of differentiated dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This refers to internal realization. The phrase "as if there were" below refers to external application. The preceding [passage] refers to the two types of wisdom: direct perception and inference.
In terms of the characteristics of realization, it is the fruit; in terms of its manifesting function, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is said "also.
This is because the functions of these two types of wisdom are able to manifest the meanings of permanence and impermanence. △ Five: Pseudo-perceptual Cognition (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).

There is conceptual cognition that functions with respect to an object in a manner different from its true nature; this is termed "pseudo-perception. That is to say, various cognitions arise through the conceptualization of jars, garments, and so forth.
Because such cognitions do not take the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as their objective domain, they are termed pseudo-perception.
This is pseudo-perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣābhāsa-jñāna*), which is precisely the cognition involved within the context of pseudo-establishment and refutation (*sādhanābhāsa-pratiṣedhābhāsa*).

To say it is "pseudo-perceptual" means that it is a conceptual cognition (*savikalpa-jñāna*) that cannot directly realize the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; rather, it functions by conceptually differentiating among the objects (*artha*) of phenomena.
Consequently, it incurs various faults within pseudo-establishment and refutation, and is thus termed "pseudo-perceptual. It differs [from true perception].

Regarding "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*): The *Dàochào* states that to perceive things such as male and female, heaven and earth, and so forth, as a "unified whole" (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*) is called "semblance direct perception.

As for a "unified whole," because it is a confluence of various conditions, one gathers together many subtle particles to form matter and combines the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) to form a person;
this is called a unified whole. To perceive in this manner is a conceptualizing cognition (*savikalpajñāna*) that functions erroneously with respect to its object.
If a "unified aggregate" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended, then true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) likewise cannot be apprehended.

As the *Vajracchedikā-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata speaks of a unified aggregate, yet it is not a unified aggregate; because it arises from the conjunction of conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This nature of being without intrinsic nature is the reality to be realized. To know it thus is the arising of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*); this is [the state of] self-... [realization].
When these are transformed through mutual engagement, it is called true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). △ Sixth, pseudo-inference (*tarka*):

If a cognition of a pseudo-reason (*hetu*) arises first, and subsequently gives rise to various cognitions of pseudo-objects, this is called pseudo-inference. There are many types of reasons for valid cognition (*pramāṇa-hetu*).

As previously stated, when cognition arises with respect to that which appears to be the object of inference, taking that [fallacious reason] as its cause, and yet fails to provide correct understanding,
it is termed "pseudo-inference" (anumānābhāsa).
That which resembles inference (*anumānābhāsa*) refers to a cognition based on a reason that is not authentic;

because it cannot penetrate the fundamental cause of phenomena, it is inverted and confused regarding the object to be inferred (*sādhyārtha*), and thus cannot bring about correct understanding in the listener. This is termed "pseudo-inference.

Its various types include, as mentioned before, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*). Consequently, the cognition that gives rise to these is termed a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*).
The cognition that arises is called "resembling the object. That which precedes it is the prior conceptualization (*pūrva-vikalpa*). △ 7. True Refutation (*bhūta-dūṣaṇa*).
